rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Urgent **thick smear detects parasites; thin smear identifies species and quantifies parasitemia**
Negative initial smear + suspicion → repeat every 12–24 h, total 3 sets
Rapid antigen test supplements microscopy; CBC, glucose, creatinine, bilirubin, lactate assess organ injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe disease → **IV artesunate**, ICU support, then complete oral regimen; never delay for species identification
Falciparum/unknown → artemether-lumefantrine; **CDC 2026: 5 days**, formerly 3; initially hospitalize
Chloroquine-sensitive vivax/ovale → chloroquine; resistant acquisition → artemether-lumefantrine
★ Anti-relapse: **primaquine or tafenoquine only after quantitative G6PD testing**; avoid during pregnancy
Pregnant vivax/ovale → defer liver-stage treatment; suppressive chloroquine after acute treatment when susceptible

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral malaria, severe anemia, renal failure, death
Artesunate → delayed hemolysis; CBC weekly for 4 weeks

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **DEET, permethrin-treated clothing/nets**; destination-specific prophylaxis before, during, and after exposure
Pregnancy: chloroquine where sensitive; mefloquine for chloroquine-resistant, mefloquine-susceptible destinations

rows.label: Mimics
items: Babesiosis: tick exposure, Maltese-cross tetrads; no hepatic stage
Dengue: marked myalgias, leukopenia, capillary leak; no intraerythrocytic parasites
Typhoid: sustained fever, abdominal symptoms; blood cultures positive

table.title: Common prophylaxis
rows: Severe renal impairment; pregnancy generally avoided

marfan-syndrome.name: Marfan syndrome
marfan-syndrome.scope: FBN1 mutation, fibrillin-1, ectopia lentis, aortic root dilatation, aortic dissection, mitral valve prolapse, echocardiographic monitoring
marfan-syndrome.core: Tall patient with long limbs, superotemporal lens displacement, and aortic root enlargement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal dominant inheritance; de novo cases possible

rows.label: Clues
items: Arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, scoliosis, disproportionate arm span
Mitral valve prolapse: midsystolic click, late systolic murmur
★ Abrupt severe chest or back pain → suspect aortic dissection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **FBN1** variant → abnormal fibrillin-1 microfibrils, weak aortic media and lens zonules

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TTE** at diagnosis, at 6 months, then annually if stable; CT/MRI if inadequate visualization
No family history: aortic root Z-score ≥2 plus ectopia lentis usually establishes diagnosis
Systemic score ≥7 or pathogenic FBN1 variant can support diagnosis with aortic root dilation
Slit-lamp exam for lens subluxation; CTA for suspected acute dissection if stable

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Beta blocker or ARB** to slow aortic enlargement
Prophylactic root replacement at ≥5.0 cm; ≥4.5 cm with rapid growth or family history of dissection
Acute type A dissection → IV esmolol and emergency surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Aortic regurgitation, rupture, tamponade; spontaneous pneumothorax
Retinal detachment or refractive impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: First-degree relative evaluation; preconception aortic assessment; avoid heavy isometric exertion and collision sports

rows.label: Mimics
items: Homocystinuria: inferonasal lens displacement, thrombosis, developmental delay
Loeys-Dietz: bifid uvula, hypertelorism, arterial tortuosity

measures-of-association.name: Measures of association
measures-of-association.scope: Relative risk (RR), odds ratio (OR), attributable risk (AR), absolute risk reduction (ARR), number needed to treat (NNT), number needed to harm (NNH), hazard ratio
measures-of-association.core: Relative measures describe proportional associations; absolute measures incorporate baseline risk and determine treatment benefit or harm.

rows.label: Definition
items: CER = control event rate; EER = experimental event rate
Two-by-two table: exposed events/non-events a/b; unexposed events/non-events c/d
Relative risk reduction (RRR; vaccine efficacy) = (CER − EER)/CER = 1 − RR

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ Ratio null = **1**; risk-difference null = **0**
★ Hazard ratio compares instantaneous event rates over time; not cumulative risk ratio
NNT/NNH require specified outcome and follow-up duration; always round up

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ RR: cohort/RCT; OR: case-control and logistic regression
Attributable risk: excess incidence among exposed attributable to exposure, assuming causality
HR: survival analysis with censoring; constant interpretation assumes proportional hazards

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Use proportions, not percentage numbers, in reciprocal calculations
OR approximates RR only with rare outcomes; common outcomes exaggerate relative association
Association alone cannot establish causality; confounding can distort every measure

measures-of-association.evidence: Statistical definitions; no clinical guideline involved.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adults: **S. pneumoniae** most common; seeded by pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis, CSF leak, asplenia
Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; advanced HIV/transplant/chemotherapy → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: subacute, high opening pressure ± CN VI palsy, CSF antigen; TB studies if lymphocytic, low glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal contacts within 7 days of onset → **rifampin or ceftriaxone**; droplet isolation until 24 hours treated
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

microcytic-anemia.name: Microcytic anemia
microcytic-anemia.scope: Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia
microcytic-anemia.core: Low hemoglobin with MCV <80 fL: distinguish depleted iron, inflammatory iron sequestration, globin underproduction, and defective heme synthesis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Menstrual/GI blood loss, pregnancy, low intake, malabsorption → iron depletion
Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy → inflammatory anemia
Inherited hemoglobin disorders; alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia → disordered heme production
Preterm birth → low stores, screen toddlers; infant microcytosis → **dietary history** for excess cow's milk

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea; severe anemia → tachycardia, angina, syncope
Pica, koilonychia, restless legs suggest iron deficiency
Markedly low MCV, preserved hemoglobin, high RBC count, **normal RDW** (Mentzer <13) suggest thalassemia trait

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin suppression, impaired absorption and iron release; cytokines blunt **erythropoietin**
Sideroblasts: mitochondrial iron accumulation in erythroblasts from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear → ferritin**, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation
★ Ferritin **<45 ng/mL in anemia** supports iron deficiency; normal result cannot exclude during inflammation
★ Adult men/postmenopausal women with iron deficiency → **EGD + colonoscopy**; consider celiac testing
Hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected beta-thalassemia; alpha trait may require genetic testing; exposure → blood lead
Microcytosis + afebrile pain crisis, at-risk ancestry → **smear** for sickled cells (sickle–β-thalassemia)

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Iron deficiency → **oral ferrous sulfate**; intolerance/malabsorption or rapid replacement need → IV iron
Treat bleeding source; continue iron about 3 months beyond hemoglobin normalization; reassess nonresponse
Inflammatory anemia → treat underlying disease; selected CKD → iron ± erythropoietin
Sideroblastic: remove trigger, pyridoxine if isoniazid-related; severe thalassemia → transfusion/chelation

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency: developmental effects in children, adverse pregnancy outcomes
Repeated transfusion → iron overload, cardiac/hepatic injury; oral iron → constipation, dark stool
Four-gene α-deletion → **Hb Barts** (γ4) → severe fetal anemia, hydrops fetalis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate dietary iron, pregnancy supplementation, lead-exposure reduction
★ **No empiric long-term iron for thalassemia trait** without documented deficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute blood loss: initially normocytic; hemoglobin may lag volume loss
Hemolysis: reticulocytosis, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin

microcytic-anemia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA iron deficiency evaluation 2020](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/); remaining hematology established teaching.

mood-stabilizers.name: Mood stabilizers
mood-stabilizers.scope: Lithium (therapeutic range, toxicity, hemodialysis, tremor, nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism), valproate (hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity), carbamazepine, lamotrigine (Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
mood-stabilizers.core: Match the drug to bipolar phase; narrow therapeutic windows, organ toxicity, interactions, and pregnancy risks drive selection.

rows.label: Use
items: Lithium: mania, maintenance, reduced suicide risk; valproate/carbamazepine: acute mania
Lamotrigine: bipolar depression prevention; ineffective for acute mania

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Lithium alters intracellular signaling; anticonvulsants reduce excitatory neurotransmission

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Lithium: **nephrogenic DI**, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism; fine tremor → **propranolol**
Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, weight gain
★ **Lamotrigine rash → stop immediately**; Stevens-Johnson risk increases with rapid titration

rows.label: Avoid
items: Valproate in pregnancy: neural tube defects, impaired neurodevelopment; carbamazepine also teratogenic
Lithium: severe renal impairment, dehydration; pregnancy counseling includes fetal cardiac risk

rows.label: Interactions
items: Thiazides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, NSAIDs increase lithium; volume depletion worsens toxicity
Carbamazepine: CYP induction, reduced contraceptive efficacy; valproate increases lamotrigine levels

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Lithium **12-hour trough**: maintenance usually 0.6–1.0; acute mania 0.8–1.2 mEq/L
Renal function, TSH, calcium; valproate CBC/LFTs; carbamazepine CBC, sodium, LFTs
Carbamazepine: HLA-B*1502 testing with relevant Asian ancestry; agranulocytosis, SIADH, severe rash

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Lithium toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion → stop lithium, IV saline
**Hemodialysis**: seizures/coma, life-threatening arrhythmia, or renal impairment with lithium >4 mEq/L
Consider dialysis: >5 mEq/L, confusion, or clearance >36 hours to <1; monitor rebound

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.name: Multiple endocrine neoplasia
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.scope: MEN1 (pituitary, parathyroid hyperplasia, pancreatic neuroendocrine), MEN2A (medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid), MEN2B (medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas), RET gene
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.core: Autosomal dominant syndromes with characteristic combinations of endocrine tumors, often multifocal and presenting young.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Affected relatives, young-onset endocrine tumor, multifocal disease, or multiple endocrine organs involved

rows.label: Clues
items: MEN1: hypercalcemia, recurrent ulcers or hypoglycemia, galactorrhea or visual field loss
MEN2B: marfanoid habitus and intestinal ganglioneuromatosis; early aggressive thyroid disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ MEN1: loss of menin tumor suppressor; MEN2: activating **RET** proto-oncogene variant

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Germline testing when phenotype suggests MEN; offer cascade testing to relatives
MEN1: calcium/PTH, prolactin and symptom-directed hormone assays; pancreatic and pituitary imaging
MEN2: calcitonin for medullary disease; plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines for pheochromocytoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pheochromocytoma → **alpha blockade then adrenal surgery before thyroid surgery**; beta blockade only after alpha
MEN1: multigland parathyroid surgery, cabergoline for prolactinoma, individualized pancreatic NET management

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypercalcemic nephrolithiasis, pituitary mass effects, metastatic NET or medullary thyroid cancer
Unrecognized pheochromocytoma → perioperative hypertensive crisis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ RET carriers → **prophylactic thyroidectomy** timed by variant risk; MEN2B generally in infancy
Genotype-directed surveillance for asymptomatic carriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia: lifelong mild hypercalcemia with low urinary calcium
Marfan syndrome: ectopia lentis and aortic root dilation

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.evidence: Established MEN teaching; current surveillance guidance not checked online.

multiple-gestation.name: Multiple gestation
multiple-gestation.scope: Dichorionic diamniotic (lambda sign), monochorionic diamniotic (T-sign), monochorionic monoamniotic, twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), selective FGR, delivery timing recommendations
multiple-gestation.core: Chorionicity and amnionicity determine twin-specific surveillance, complications, and delivery timing; establish both on first-trimester ultrasound.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dizygotic twins: ovulation induction/assisted reproduction, maternal age, family history
Monozygotic splitting timing determines placental and sac sharing

rows.label: Clues
items: Uterus larger than dates, exaggerated pregnancy symptoms; ultrasound confirms fetal number
★ Shared placenta with **oligohydramnios/polyhydramnios sequence** → TTTS; small/absent donor bladder
Selective FGR: one small twin, discordant estimated weights; assess each umbilical artery Doppler

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental vascular anastomoses permit imbalanced flow in monochorionic twins
Donor hypovolemia reduces urine; recipient hypervolemia increases urine and cardiac strain

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **First-trimester ultrasound** identifies shared placenta and intertwin membrane
Monochorionic diamniotic → ultrasound **every 2 weeks from 16 weeks** for fluid/bladders
Serial growth in all twins; Doppler and more frequent assessment when growth discordance develops
TTTS donor deepest pocket ≤2 cm, recipient ≥8 cm; staging incorporates bladder, Doppler, hydrops

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ TTTS stages II–IV at 16–26 weeks → **fetoscopic laser ablation** of placental anastomoses
Asymptomatic stage I → at least weekly surveillance; refer fetal intervention center if progression/symptoms
★ Diamniotic twins with **first twin cephalic** may deliver vaginally with experienced team
Monoamniotic twins → cesarean; fetal deterioration, preeclampsia, or severe growth issues may require earlier delivery

rows.label: Complications
items: Preterm birth, preeclampsia, anemia, gestational diabetes, postpartum hemorrhage
Monoamniotic cord entanglement; monochorionic co-twin death can cause surviving twin neurologic injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention; optimize iron/nutrition; single-embryo transfer reduces iatrogenic multiples

rows.label: Mimics
items: Incorrect dates/macrosomia: enlarged uterus but singleton on imaging
Twin anemia-polycythemia sequence: discordant MCA velocities without major fluid imbalance

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.name: Neonatal intestinal obstruction
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.scope: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, bilious vomiting, upper GI contrast series, Ladd procedure
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.core: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proved otherwise; volvulus must be excluded before bowel ischemia develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Polyhydramnios → prenatal proximal obstruction; Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
CF → meconium ileus; trisomy 21 → Hirschsprung disease
Prematurity increases alternative risk of necrotizing enterocolitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Proximal obstruction → early vomiting with little distention; distal obstruction → marked distention
No meconium by **48 hours**, explosive stool after rectal exam → distal aganglionosis
★ Bloody stool, tenderness, shock or metabolic acidosis → ischemic bowel; urgent surgery
Volvulus: sudden bilious emesis after normal feeding and meconium; atresia: vomiting from first feeds

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malrotation leaves narrow mesenteric base → twisting of bowel and mesenteric blood supply
Duodenal atresia: failed recanalization; jejunoileal atresia: fetal vascular injury
Hirschsprung: absent enteric ganglia → failure of distal relaxation and proximal dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal radiograph** first; double bubble without distal gas supports duodenal atresia
★ Suspected malrotation, stable → **upper GI contrast series**; corkscrew/abnormal DJ junction; enema: misplaced cecum
Distal obstruction → contrast enema to characterize microcolon, meconium or transition zone
Hirschsprung confirmation → **rectal suction biopsy**, absent ganglion cells
Peritonitis or unstable suspected volvulus → exploration without delaying for contrast

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All suspected obstruction → **NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids**, pediatric surgery
Volvulus → emergency Ladd procedure, detorsion and viability assessment; broad antibiotics if ischemic
Atresias → operative repair after stabilization; duodenal repair commonly duodenoduodenostomy
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → water-soluble contrast enema with hydration; complicated cases → surgery
Hirschsprung → irrigations then pull-through; enterocolitis → fluids, decompression, IV broad antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, short-bowel syndrome; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can be fatal
Delayed diagnosis causes aspiration, electrolyte depletion and growth failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile emesis at several weeks
NEC: ill preterm infant, pneumatosis intestinalis
Physiologic reflux: thriving infant without bile or distention

table.title: Distal obstruction clues
rows: Narrow distal segment, proximal transition zone

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal surgical teaching.

neurocutaneous-disorders.name: Neurocutaneous disorders
neurocutaneous-disorders.scope: Neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease, ataxia-telangiectasia
neurocutaneous-disorders.core: Characteristic skin or ocular lesions plus neurologic tumors, seizures, or progressive ataxia suggest an inherited or mosaic multisystem disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, TSC, VHL: autosomal dominant; frequent de novo variants
Ataxia-telangiectasia: autosomal recessive; Sturge-Weber: sporadic somatic mosaicism

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Changing painful neurofibroma**, rapid growth, or new weakness → malignant transformation concern
Early focal seizures or developmental regression → evaluate structural cerebral lesions
NF2: hearing loss/tinnitus; NF1: cutaneous neurofibromas and childhood learning difficulties

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor suppressor dysfunction → hamartomas or neoplasms; ATM defect → impaired DNA repair

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical pattern + genetic testing**; targeted MRI for neurologic or tumor symptoms
NF1: ≥2 criteria; ≥6 café-au-lait macules, size >5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal
TSC: two major features or one major plus two minor; pathogenic variant also diagnostic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic tumors → specialist resection; TSC growing lesions → **everolimus** in selected cases
TSC infantile spasms → vigabatrin; other seizures → antiseizure drugs
Sturge-Weber seizures → levetiracetam; refractory focal epilepsy → surgical evaluation
Ataxia-telangiectasia: rehabilitation, infection treatment; minimize ionizing radiation

rows.label: Complications
items: NF1: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor; VHL: renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
TSC: hydrocephalus, renal hemorrhage; ataxia-telangiectasia: lymphoma/leukemia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**; syndrome-specific eye, hearing, renal, and tumor surveillance
Sturge-Weber: ophthalmology follow-up for glaucoma; NF1: childhood BP and vision monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Isolated café-au-lait macules: no additional diagnostic criteria
Friedreich ataxia: areflexia, cardiomyopathy, no ocular telangiectasias

table.title: Signature findings
rows: Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma
Ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas, cortical tubers, renal angiomyolipomas

neurocutaneous-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical genetics teaching.

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.name: Neuromuscular junction disorders
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.scope: Myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism, repetitive nerve stimulation, autoantibodies
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.core: Fluctuating or descending weakness with preserved sensation localizes to neuromuscular transmission; reflexes, pupils, and exercise response separate major causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: MG: autoimmune disease, thymoma; LEMS: smoking/small-cell lung carcinoma
Botulism: improperly canned foods, injection wounds, infant honey or environmental spores

rows.label: Clues
items: MG: diplopia, ptosis, nasal speech, chewing fatigue; worse late day or repeated activity
LEMS: proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation; transient strength/reflex improvement after exertion
Botulism: cranial palsies → symmetric descending paralysis, autonomic dysfunction; infant constipation and floppy weakness
★ **Bulbar weakness or declining ventilation** → impending respiratory failure even with normal oxygen saturation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: MG: postsynaptic receptor/MuSK autoimmunity; LEMS: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel autoimmunity
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → impaired acetylcholine release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AChR antibodies**, then MuSK if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG
MG → chest CT for thymoma; bedside ice-pack improvement supports ocular disease
LEMS → P/Q calcium-channel antibodies and chest CT for cancer
★ Suspected crisis → serial **forced vital capacity/negative inspiratory force**; not pulse oximetry alone
Botulism → serum/stool/toxin testing via public health; treatment before confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: MG → pyridostigmine, steroid-sparing immunosuppression; thymectomy for thymoma or selected generalized AChR-positive disease
★ Myasthenic crisis → **airway support + IVIG or plasma exchange**, treat precipitant
LEMS → amifampridine and treatment of malignancy; immunotherapy for persistent autoimmune disease
★ Botulism → **heptavalent antitoxin**; infants → human botulism immune globulin; ventilatory support
Wound botulism → debridement/antibiotics; avoid aminoglycosides and magnesium with impaired junctional transmission

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, respiratory arrest; MG immunosuppression → infection; steroids may initially worsen weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review MG-exacerbating drugs; safe food preservation; no honey before age 1 year
LEMS → ongoing cancer surveillance if initial evaluation negative

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: usually ascending weakness and areflexia, possible sensory symptoms
Brainstem stroke: abrupt focal signs; motor neuron disease: fasciculations/UMN signs

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.evidence: Botulism checked 2026-10-30: [CDC clinical guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7002a1.htm); MG/LEMS: established teaching.

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.name: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.scope: COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition mechanism, renal adverse effects (sodium retention, acute kidney injury), gastrointestinal toxicity, cardiovascular risks
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.core: NSAIDs reduce pain, inflammation, and fever through cyclooxygenase inhibition, with gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular tradeoffs.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Pain, dysmenorrhea, renal colic, gout; **lowest effective dose, shortest duration**
Topical diclofenac for localized joint pain reduces systemic exposure

rows.label: Mechanism
items: COX-1: gastric/platelet/renal effects; COX-2: inflammatory prostaglandins and endothelial prostacyclin
Most reversibly inhibit enzymes; aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ ↓Prostaglandin/prostacyclin → **afferent arteriolar constriction** → AKI, hyperkalemia, sodium retention, hypertension/HF worsening
★ Gastritis, **ulcer/bleeding**; platelet inhibition except with selective COX-2 agents
MI/stroke; interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy (chronic daily use, papillary necrosis); bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma

rows.label: Avoid
items: Active GI bleeding, severe CKD, decompensated HF, peri-CABG setting
Pregnancy ≥20 weeks generally avoid; later gestation → ductal closure and fetal renal injury
Aspirin in children with viral illness → Reye syndrome

rows.label: Interactions
items: ★ ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID → **high AKI risk**
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets → bleeding; NSAIDs can increase lithium and methotrexate exposure

rows.label: Monitor
items: BP, edema, creatinine, K; assess melena/anemia and prior ulcer history
High GI risk → consider PPI; reassess need rather than automatically continuing indefinitely
Rising creatinine or BP → stop NSAID, switch to **acetaminophen**

rows.label: Traps
items: Celecoxib reduces GI/platelet effects but retains renal and thrombotic risks
Prescribed low-dose aspirin for obstetric indications remains an exception to pregnancy NSAID restriction
Do not combine multiple NSAIDs for additional analgesia

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.evidence: Pregnancy safety checked 2026-10-30: [FDA NSAID warning](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-recommends-avoiding-use-nsaids-pregnancy-20-weeks-or-later-because-they-can-result-low-amniotic); other pharmacology: established teaching.

nutritional-deficiencies.name: Nutritional deficiencies
nutritional-deficiencies.scope: Vegan diet nutrient risks, tea-and-toast diet, vitamin and mineral supplementation, clinical manifestations
nutritional-deficiencies.core: Restricted intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements produce characteristic mucocutaneous, neurologic, hematologic, and skeletal findings; identify the missing nutrient and its cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupplemented vegan diet: B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc risks
Tea-and-toast diet, alcohol misuse, food insecurity, restrictive eating, institutionalization
Bariatric surgery, pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, bowel disease → specific or fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor wound healing, bruising, oral changes, neuropathy, bone pain; mixed deficiencies commonly coexist
★ **Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia** in malnutrition → thiamine deficiency; complete triad often absent
Night blindness → vitamin A; bleeding with prolonged PT → vitamin K
Dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia → niacin; periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, dysgeusia → zinc (TPN, penicillamine)

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient cofactors impair energy metabolism, collagen formation, hematopoiesis, or mineralization
Low intake differs from malabsorption: replacement route and lasting supplementation must match the mechanism
Vitamin D deficiency → ↓calcium absorption → **secondary hyperparathyroidism**: normal calcium at bone's expense

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diet and supplement history**, weight trend, oral/skin/neurologic examination; assess GI disease
CBC/ferritin, B12 ± methylmalonic acid, 25-OH vitamin D chosen by findings; avoid indiscriminate panels
Albumin is altered by inflammation/fluid status; not a stand-alone nutrition diagnostic test
Severely undernourished → baseline phosphate, Mg, K before nutritional rehabilitation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke syndrome → **parenteral thiamine promptly**; do not await laboratory confirmation
B12 deficiency with neurologic signs/malabsorption → parenteral replacement; folate only after B12 assessment
Vitamin D/calcium for deficient intake or osteomalacia; iron replacement with evaluation for blood loss
Vitamin C for scurvy; oral balanced nutrition plus cause-directed supplementation and dietitian support
★ Severe malnutrition → **slow refeeding + thiamine**, close phosphate/K/Mg monitoring and replacement

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible B12 neurologic injury, fractures, anemia, infection susceptibility
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia, respiratory failure; excess vitamin A → hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vegans → **reliable B12 supplementation**; fortified foods, calcium/vitamin D and iodine adequacy
Diversified diet, food access support, lifelong bariatric follow-up; avoid megadose supplementation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Scurvy versus vasculitis: perifollicular hemorrhage/corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, restricted produce intake
Hypothyroidism: fatigue and macrocytosis with elevated TSH

nutritional-deficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established nutritional deficiency and refeeding principles.

obesity-hypoventilation-syndrome.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
obesity-hypoventilation-syndrome.scope: Alveolar hypoventilation, daytime hypercapnia, normal A-a gradient hypoxemia, cor pulmonale, positive airway pressure
obesity-hypoventilation-syndrome.core: Obesity with awake hypercapnia after exclusion of alternative causes defines obesity hypoventilation syndrome, usually accompanied by obstructive sleep apnea.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Severe obesity, coexistent sleep-disordered breathing; sedatives/opioids may precipitate decompensation
Reduced mobility, cardiopulmonary comorbidity and weight gain increase ventilatory load

rows.label: Clues
items: Daytime somnolence, morning headache, snoring, nocturia; dyspnea/awake hypoxemia suggest more than isolated OSA
Elevated bicarbonate reflects renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis
Peripheral edema, JVD and loud P2 suggest pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale
★ Acute lethargy, worsening acidosis or respiratory distress → **acute-on-chronic hypercapnic failure**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chest-wall load, reduced compliance and blunted ventilatory drive cause inadequate alveolar ventilation
Pure hypoventilation produces hypoxemia with normal A–a gradient; atelectasis/comorbidity may increase the gradient

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **BMI ≥30 + awake PaCO2 ≥45 mm Hg**, excluding other hypoventilation causes
★ Low/moderate suspicion and **bicarbonate <27 mmol/L** → OHS unlikely; ≥27 → ABG
Strong suspicion → ABG directly; pulse oximetry alone cannot diagnose ventilatory failure
Polysomnography defines OSA severity and guides PAP settings; assess spirometry, thyroid and drug causes
Exclude COPD, neuromuscular weakness, chest-wall disorders and central hypoventilation before assigning diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stable with severe OSA → **CPAP first-line**; persistent hypercapnia or nonobstructive hypoventilation → bilevel PAP
Acute hypercapnic decompensation → **bilevel noninvasive ventilation** if protecting airway; intubate if failing
Hospitalized suspected OHS with respiratory failure → discharge NIV pending prompt sleep assessment/titration
★ Sustained **weight loss**, often bariatric treatment, provides definitive disease modification
Avoid oxygen alone: can worsen CO2 retention; add oxygen only for residual hypoxemia despite adequate ventilation

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, right-heart failure, recurrent respiratory admissions and increased mortality
Anesthesia/opioids increase perioperative hypoventilation risk; monitor ventilation after procedures

rows.label: Prevention
items: PAP adherence, weight management and avoidance of respiratory depressants
Coordinate sleep follow-up and cardiometabolic treatment; counsel against drowsy driving

rows.label: Mimics
items: Isolated OSA: daytime PaCO2 generally normal
COPD: obstructive spirometry and smoking history
Neuromuscular weakness: reduced respiratory strength without obesity requirement

opioid-toxicity.name: Opioid toxicity
opioid-toxicity.scope: Opioid toxidrome, naloxone administration and titration, observation period, precipitated withdrawal
opioid-toxicity.core: Depressed consciousness, slow breathing, and pinpoint pupils after opioid exposure; ventilation takes priority over full awakening.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fentanyl or heroin exposure, dose escalation, renal dysfunction, long-acting opioids
Alcohol/benzodiazepine co-ingestion; lost tolerance after detoxification, hospitalization, or incarceration

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Bradypnea or apnea** with hypoxemia; reduced bowel sounds, bradycardia, hypotension
Miosis may be absent with severe hypoxia or co-ingestion; needle marks are not required
Pulmonary edema, aspiration, hypothermia, prolonged immobilization may accompany overdose
Chronic use: daytime sleepiness, constipation, apathy, falling grades, miosis, slow breathing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mu-receptor activation suppresses medullary ventilatory response to CO2
Naloxone competitively reverses opioid effects but often wears off before the causative opioid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bedside glucose, pulse oximetry, capnography; do not await toxicology
Urine opiate immunoassay detects morphine/heroin/codeine; may miss fentanyl, methadone, and oxycodone
ECG for methadone-associated QT prolongation; acetaminophen level with uncertain combination-product ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open airway, **bag-mask ventilation**, oxygen; intubate if ventilation cannot be maintained
★ **Naloxone** IV titrated to adequate breathing; intranasal/IM route if IV unavailable
Dependent but breathing: start low; apnea/no response: prompt larger/repeated doses, especially fentanyl analogs
Repeated recurrence → naloxone infusion; coma despite repeated doses → evaluate additional causes
Short-acting reversal: observe ≥4 hours after last naloxone; long-acting/recurrent sedation → prolonged monitoring/admission

rows.label: Complications
items: Anoxic brain injury, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome
Precipitated withdrawal: agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia; rare pulmonary edema after reversal

rows.label: Prevention
items: Take-home naloxone, overdose-response training, avoid sedative combinations; offer buprenorphine and addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pontine hemorrhage: focal neurologic findings, no meaningful naloxone response
Clonidine poisoning: marked bradycardia with similar pupils
Sedative overdose: usually normal pupils; incomplete naloxone response

orbital-and-preseptal-cellulitis.name: Orbital and preseptal cellulitis
orbital-and-preseptal-cellulitis.scope: Preseptal cellulitis, orbital cellulitis, ethmoid sinusitis complication, pain with extraocular movements, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, CT scan of orbits, intravenous antibiotics
orbital-and-preseptal-cellulitis.core: Eyelid erythema and edema with orbital signs indicate a postseptal emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Orbital: contiguous spread from ethmoid sinusitis; preseptal: skin trauma, insect bite, hordeolum

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Pain with extraocular movements** suggests orbital spread even before vision declines
Relative afferent pupillary defect or color desaturation → optic nerve compromise
Chemosis, fever and systemic illness support deeper infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Orbital septum separates superficial lid infection from orbital fat and extraocular muscles
Thin lamina papyracea permits ethmoid infection to spread into medial orbit

rows.label: Dx
items: Document visual acuity, pupils, motility and globe position; assess for systemic toxicity
★ Orbital signs or inadequate exam → **contrast CT of orbits and sinuses**; MRI for intracranial concern
Uncomplicated preseptal infection with reliable exam usually clinical

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Orbital: admit; urgent ophthalmology/ENT; **IV vancomycin plus ceftriaxone**, add metronidazole for anaerobic concern
Visual compromise, significant abscess, intracranial extension or deterioration → urgent drainage assessment
★ Mild preseptal: oral amoxicillin-clavulanate with close follow-up; admit if toxic or unreliable follow-up

rows.label: Complications
items: Subperiosteal abscess, permanent blindness, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis or brain abscess

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prompt care of infected wounds and bacterial sinusitis; routine Hib and pneumococcal immunization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Allergic eyelid edema: itching, often bilateral and afebrile
Cavernous sinus thrombosis: severe headache, cranial nerve palsies, often bilateral progression

orbital-and-preseptal-cellulitis.evidence: Checked AAO clinical resources on orbital and preseptal cellulitis.

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.scope: Clinical diagnosis (Heberden/Bouchard nodes, activity-related pain), radiographic findings, nonpharmacologic therapy, oral and topical NSAIDs, injections
osteoarthritis.core: Activity-related joint pain with brief morning stiffness, crepitus and bony enlargement suggests degenerative joint disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, **obesity** (strongest modifiable), prior trauma, malalignment, repetitive occupational loading
Family history, particularly hand disease; obesity affects both mechanical and metabolic risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning stiffness generally **<30 minutes**; pain improves with rest early in disease
Knees, hips, first carpometacarpal, DIP and PIP commonly involved; MCP usually spared
Heberden nodes: DIP; Bouchard nodes: PIP; reduced motion and varus/valgus deformity
Hip disease: groin pain with restricted internal rotation; referred pain can localize to knee

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Articular cartilage loss, subchondral remodeling and osteophytes; low-grade synovial inflammation
Joint pain arises from innervated surrounding structures rather than aneural cartilage itself

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical presentation → **clinical diagnosis**; imaging unnecessary for straightforward mild disease
Weight-bearing radiographs if uncertain, severe or worsening: asymmetric joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts
★ Hot acutely swollen joint → **arthrocentesis**; not an OA flare; mild cool effusion → x-ray, simple analgesic
OA fluid noninflammatory: usually WBC <2000/µL; inflammatory markers generally normal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **exercise, strengthening, weight loss**; cane contralateral to painful hip/knee
★ Knee/hand pain → **topical diclofenac**; oral NSAID if insufficient and renal/GI/CV risks acceptable
Acetaminophen if unable to use NSAIDs (older exam questions may expect it first); duloxetine for persistent pain
Intra-articular glucocorticoid for short-term relief; avoid routine opioids and hyaluronic acid injections
Severe pain/function loss despite conservative treatment → **joint replacement**

rows.label: Complications
items: Functional limitation, falls, reduced activity and secondary deconditioning
NSAIDs → GI bleeding, AKI, fluid retention; arthroplasty → infection or VTE

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Weight loss** best prevents knee OA, beyond exercise alone; conditioning, injury prevention; no complete joint rest

rows.label: Mimics
items: Rheumatoid arthritis: prolonged stiffness, boggy symmetric MCP/wrist synovitis, marginal erosions, DIP spared
CPPD: acute inflammatory flares, chondrocalcinosis
Septic arthritis: fever, severe painful passive motion, positive synovial culture
Trochanteric bursitis: lateral hip pain over greater trochanter, not groin pain

osteoarthritis.evidence: Not checked online; established ACR/Arthritis Foundation principles.

osteomyelitis.name: Osteomyelitis
osteomyelitis.scope: Vertebral osteomyelitis and discitis, hematogenous seeding (S. aureus, IV drug use), contiguous spread (diabetic foot ulcer), probe-to-bone test, MRI, bone biopsy and culture, parenteral antibiotics
osteomyelitis.core: Persistent focal bone or back pain, especially with bacteremia, a deep diabetic ulcer, or elevated inflammatory markers, suggests bone infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hematogenous seeding: S. aureus, endocarditis, injection drug use; vertebral disease often lacks fever
Contiguous spread: diabetic foot ulcers, pressure injury; direct inoculation: open fracture, surgery, hardware
Sickle cell: Salmonella association, but S. aureus remains important; plantar puncture through shoe → Pseudomonas

rows.label: Clues
items: Point tenderness, swelling, drainage or nonhealing sinus; systemic toxicity may be absent
★ New neurologic deficit, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention → **epidural extension/cord compression**
Diabetic ulcer over bony prominence, visible bone, or prolonged failure to heal increases suspicion
Child: fever, point tenderness over long-bone **metaphysis**; septic joint instead limits joint motion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Infected bone develops inflammatory pressure, vascular compromise, and necrosis
Sequestrum: devitalized infected bone; involucrum: reactive new bone; biofilm promotes hardware persistence

rows.label: Dx
items: CBC, ESR/CRP, two blood-culture sets; plain films first but early findings can be absent
★ Diabetic foot: **probe-to-bone** plus radiographs/inflammatory markers; MRI if diagnosis remains uncertain
★ **MRI** best for early marrow disease and epidural/paraspinal abscess; bone scan uptake if MRI unavailable
Bone biopsy for histology/culture before antibiotics if stable; superficial wound swabs unreliable
Compatible vertebral MRI plus S. aureus bacteremia usually obviates biopsy; assess endocarditis source

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sepsis or neurologic compromise → cultures then **IV vancomycin + cefepime**, urgent surgical assessment
Stable vertebral disease → obtain microbiologic diagnosis before empiric antibiotics
MSSA → cefazolin/nafcillin; MRSA → vancomycin; tailor to cultures, usually about **6 weeks**
IV initially for serious disease; selected stable patients can complete highly bioavailable oral regimens
Debride necrotic bone/drain abscess; surgery for instability, progressive deficit, or uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Epidural abscess, pathologic fracture, deformity, bacteremia, chronic draining sinus
Longstanding sinus may develop squamous carcinoma; prolonged antibiotics → line infection, renal injury, C. difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Diabetic foot inspection, offloading, vascular assessment, glucose control; prompt open-fracture antibiotics and debridement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Charcot arthropathy: neuropathic warm foot, joint fragmentation; MRI/biopsy may distinguish overlapping infection
Bone malignancy: destructive mass, pathology without infection
Degenerative disc disease: mechanical pain without infectious endplate/disc pattern

ovarian-cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian-cancer.scope: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma, CA-125, pelvic ultrasound, peritoneal carcinomatosis, germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal tumors, surgical staging and cytoreduction, platinum-based chemotherapy
ovarian-cancer.core: Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic symptoms, or an adnexal mass—especially after menopause—requires evaluation for an often late-presenting malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, nulliparity, BRCA1/2 or Lynch syndrome; family history of breast/ovarian cancer
Endometriosis associated with clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes; pregnancy and combined contraceptives reduce epithelial risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Older patient + ascites, large/fixed pelvic mass, weight loss, pleural effusion, obstruction → **epithelial** carcinoma
Young patient with rapidly enlarging mass → germ cell tumor; estrogen/androgen effects → stromal tumor
Postmenopausal bleeding with adnexal mass → consider estrogen-secreting granulosa tumor and endometrial disease
★ **Palpable ovary after menopause** → abnormal (ovaries atrophy); pelvic ultrasound

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Many high-grade serous tumors arise in distal fallopian tube epithelium
Transcoelomic seeding produces peritoneal/omental disease; hormone secretion depends on tumor lineage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Transvaginal ultrasound** first; solid components, papillary projections, vascularity, ascites increase suspicion
★ **CA-125** supports risk assessment/monitoring, not diagnosis or average-risk screening
Young/complex mass → β-hCG, AFP, LDH; suspected stromal tumor → inhibin/sex hormones
Suspected malignancy → CT abdomen/pelvis/chest and gynecologic oncology; definitive histology and staging usually surgical
Isolated resectable mass → avoid aspiration; advanced disease → biopsy before neoadjuvant chemotherapy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Epithelial carcinoma → **surgical staging/cytoreduction + carboplatin/paclitaxel** according to stage
Poor upfront surgical candidate → tissue confirmation, neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy, interval cytoreduction
Germ cell malignancy → fertility-sparing surgery when feasible; stage IA dysgerminoma may avoid chemotherapy
Higher-risk germ cell tumors → bleomycin/etoposide/cisplatin
Selected BRCA/HRD-associated disease → PARP-inhibitor maintenance after platinum response

rows.label: Complications
items: Peritoneal carcinomatosis, ascites, malignant obstruction, VTE; chemotherapy neuropathy/myelosuppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **No routine CA-125/ultrasound screening** in asymptomatic average-risk patients
Genetic counseling/testing; hereditary high-risk patients → discuss risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endometrioma: cyclic pain, ground-glass ultrasound; CA-125 can rise
Meigs syndrome: benign ovarian fibroma plus ascites/pleural effusion; no peritoneal implants

table.title: Tumor markers
rows: Often bilateral; psammoma bodies; WT1+, p53 abnormal

pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.scope: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9, neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma)
pancreatic-cancer.core: Older adult with weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice, or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, increasing age; strong family history, hereditary cancer syndromes
New diabetes with unexplained weight loss can signal occult malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Head lesions: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, nontender palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier sign**)
Body/tail lesions: late presentation with pain and cachexia; migratory thrombophlebitis may occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ductal adenocarcinoma causes biliary obstruction, perineural invasion, and early metastatic spread
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from endocrine cells; may be functional or incidental

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pancreatic-protocol CT** for mass, vessels, metastases; ultrasound may show **double-duct** (bile + pancreatic) dilation
EUS biopsy before systemic treatment/uncertain diagnosis; not mandatory before straightforward resection
★ **CA 19-9** monitors disease; neither screening nor definitive diagnosis; obstruction can falsely elevate
Resectability depends on metastases and major vascular involvement; MRI clarifies indeterminate liver lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable head tumor → **Whipple**; body/tail tumor → distal pancreatectomy; add systemic chemotherapy
Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant treatment; metastatic → systemic treatment and palliation
★ Cholangitis → **urgent ERCP**; unresectable symptomatic jaundice → biliary stent
Analgesia, pancreatic enzymes for malabsorption, nutritional support

rows.label: Complications
items: VTE, biliary infection, gastric outlet obstruction, exocrine insufficiency, diabetes
Resection → pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, malabsorption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; no average-risk population screening; selected hereditary high-risk patients → MRI/EUS surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: colicky pain, ductal stone
Autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 elevation, diffuse pancreatic enlargement
Chronic pancreatitis: calcification, recurrent pain, prior inflammation

table.title: Functional neuroendocrine tumors
rows: ↑Insulin/C-peptide during supervised fast; negative sulfonylurea screen
Massive watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, flushing

pancreatic-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established pancreatic oncology teaching.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones (prior postprandial biliary colic), heavy alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease
Blunt abdominal trauma + epigastric mass/raised enzymes → contrast CT for pancreatic/duodenal injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue: ↓insulin, ↓glucagon, normal insulin sensitivity; lipase may normalize

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase or amylase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT: diagnostic doubt, high fever/marked leukocytosis (necrosis?), deterioration, no improvement by 48–72 hours; not routine early
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency
Recurrent, no gallstones/alcohol → EUS or MRCP for ductal anatomy; older exam questions may expect ERCP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, reassessment, IV opioid analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** by 48 hours if tolerated; else enteral; older exam questions may expect initial bowel rest
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Uncomplicated/sterile: no antibiotics; infected necrosis: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancrelipase, fat-soluble vitamins, pain control; islet-loss diabetes → **insulin**, not sulfonylureas

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; necrosis, hemorrhage; **splenic vein thrombosis** → isolated gastric varices, normal liver
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

parkinson-disease.name: Parkinson disease
parkinson-disease.scope: Cardinal motor symptoms (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability/pull test), nonmotor symptoms, dopamine agonists, levodopa-carbidopa, atypical parkinsonism (PSP, MSA)
parkinson-disease.core: Progressive asymmetric bradykinesia with characteristic motor signs and levodopa responsiveness suggests Parkinson disease; early atypical features prompt another diagnosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, family susceptibility, some pesticide exposures; most disease sporadic
Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics/metoclopramide cause secondary parkinsonism rather than idiopathic disease
MPTP (synthetic heroin contaminant) → rapid parkinsonism from nigral dopaminergic neuron destruction

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity**, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait
Freezing, micrographia, hypophonia; pull test reveals impaired postural recovery, typically later
Constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression and autonomic symptoms can precede motor disease
Early severe falls, gaze palsy, marked autonomic failure or poor treatment response → atypical syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss; α-synuclein Lewy bodies
Reduced striatal dopamine disrupts basal ganglia motor regulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity
Brain MRI for atypical findings; dopamine transporter imaging if uncertain degenerative versus nondegenerative tremor
Review medications; assess cognition, orthostatic BP, gait and swallowing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Function-limiting motor symptoms → **carbidopa/levodopa**, preferred initial dopaminergic treatment
Pramipexole/ropinirole for selected younger patients; avoid with hallucinations, impulse-control problems or age >70
Wearing-off → adjust levodopa schedule, add MAO-B/COMT inhibitor; dyskinesia → amantadine
★ Exercise, PT/speech/swallow rehab; refractory fluctuations/tremor/dyskinesias → **deep brain stimulation**, pallidotomy
Psychosis → reduce provoking drugs; pimavanserin or selected quetiapine/clozapine, avoid potent dopamine blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, dementia; medication → hallucinations, orthostasis, motor fluctuations/dyskinesias
Dopamine agonists → gambling/hypersexuality and sleep attacks; abrupt withdrawal → severe rigidity/hyperthermia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall-proof home, medication adherence, aspiration-risk assessment; no established primary neuroprotective treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Essential tremor: action/postural tremor without decrementing bradykinesia
Drug-induced: blocker exposure, often symmetric; normal-pressure hydrocephalus: magnetic gait, urinary/cognitive symptoms

table.title: Atypical parkinsonism
rows: Severe orthostasis/urinary dysfunction, possible cerebellar signs
Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism

pelvic-organ-prolapse.name: Pelvic organ prolapse
pelvic-organ-prolapse.scope: Anterior compartment (cystocele), posterior compartment (rectocele, enterocele), apical compartment (uterine prolapse, vaginal vault prolapse, procidentia), pelvic floor muscle training, pessary, surgical repair
pelvic-organ-prolapse.core: Loss of pelvic support causes a vaginal bulge with pressure, urinary symptoms, or obstructed defecation, often worse when standing or straining.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Vaginal births, increasing age, menopause, obesity, connective-tissue weakness
Chronic cough/constipation, heavy lifting; hysterectomy predisposes to vaginal vault descent

rows.label: Clues
items: Visible/palpable protrusion, incomplete bladder emptying, stress leakage, need to splint vagina for defecation
★ **Urinary retention or hydronephrosis** with advanced descent → evaluate obstruction promptly
Symptoms improve supine; mucosal rubbing can produce spotting or ulceration

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Levator ani injury and fascial/ligamentous failure permit descent of one or several vaginal compartments

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pelvic examination during Valsalva**, sometimes standing; isolate compartments with speculum
POP-Q stages descent relative to hymen; measure postvoid residual when voiding symptoms present
Urinalysis for urinary symptoms; creatinine/renal ultrasound when severe obstruction suspected
Reduce prolapse during cough stress testing to unmask occult stress incontinence before surgery

rows.label: Tx
items: Asymptomatic prolapse → observation; bothersome mild disease → pelvic floor muscle training
★ **Vaginal pessary** for conservative treatment, frail/high surgical risk; fit, teach removal, schedule mucosal checks
Vaginal estrogen for atrophic mucosa when suitable; does not restore structural support
★ Persistent symptoms → compartment repair plus **apical suspension** when support deficient
No future vaginal intercourse desired → colpocleisis; preservation/reconstruction chosen according to goals

rows.label: Complications
items: Ulceration, recurrent UTI, retention, obstructive kidney injury; recurrence after repair
Neglected pessary → erosion/fistula; surgery → dyspareunia, new urinary leakage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Weight reduction, treat constipation/cough, reduce straining; pelvic floor exercises and pessary follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Urethral diverticulum: focal anterior mass, postvoid dribbling, recurrent infection
Vaginal cyst: discrete lesion without generalized descent during strain

table.title: Compartments
rows: Small bowel → upper posterior vagina/vault; peristalsis
Entire uterus prolapses beyond vaginal introitus

pelvic-organ-prolapse.evidence: Not checked online; established urogynecology evaluation and conservative/surgical management.

pertussis.name: Pertussis
pertussis.scope: Bordetella pertussis, catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, posttussive emesis, inspiratory whoop, macrolide therapy, postexposure prophylaxis, Tdap vaccination
pertussis.core: Prolonged paroxysmal cough with posttussive emesis; infants may present with apnea and cyanosis without a whoop.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unvaccinated/undervaccinated children, waning immunity in adolescents/adults, infected household contacts
Young infants have greatest risk of severe disease; vaccinated individuals can still transmit infection

rows.label: Clues
items: Catarrhal stage: rhinorrhea, mild cough, little or no fever; greatest early infectiousness
Inspiratory whoop often absent in adolescents/adults; convalescence can last weeks with recurrent cough
★ Infant **marked lymphocytosis**, poor feeding, or respiratory compromise; minimal fever despite serious illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: B. pertussis adheres to respiratory cilia; toxin-mediated injury impairs mucus clearance
Pertussis toxin inhibits Gi signaling; impaired lymphocyte extravasation causes circulating lymphocytosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Nasopharyngeal PCR** during first 3–4 weeks of cough; posterior nasopharynx, not throat swab
Culture most useful in first 2 weeks; late illness → validated serology when available
Treat suspected high-risk cases before results; chest imaging for respiratory compromise or suspected pneumonia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Azithromycin** preferred; TMP-SMX alternative at age ≥2 months when macrolides unsuitable
Best symptom benefit early; later treatment mainly reduces transmission within infectious window
Treat age ≥1 year within 3 weeks of cough; infants/pregnancy up to 6 weeks
Hospitalize young infants or apnea/hypoxemia; oxygen, suction, hydration and cardiorespiratory monitoring
Infant macrolides carry pyloric stenosis risk, but benefit outweighs risk; monitor vomiting

rows.label: Complications
items: Pneumonia, seizures/encephalopathy, infant pulmonary hypertension and death
Adults: rib fractures, syncope, stress incontinence from forceful coughing

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Droplet isolation until **5 days of effective antibiotics**, or 21 days from cough onset untreated
Household contacts → azithromycin prophylaxis within 21 days of index cough; also target high-risk exposures
DTaP childhood series; Tdap adolescent booster and once for adults without prior Tdap
★ **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 weeks**, preferably early in that interval

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral bronchitis: improving ordinary cough without characteristic paroxysms or epidemiologic link
Asthma: recurrent wheeze/trigger pattern, reversible airflow obstruction
Chlamydial infant pneumonia: afebrile staccato cough, eosinophilia, often prior conjunctivitis

pleural-effusion.name: Pleural effusion
pleural-effusion.scope: Transudate vs exudate (Light criteria), parapneumonic effusion, empyema, malignant effusion
pleural-effusion.core: Fluid in the pleural space causes dyspnea, dullness, and reduced breath sounds; classify by mechanism and identify infection requiring drainage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome; pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, TB
Recent thoracic surgery, pancreatitis, esophageal rupture, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Pleuritic pain, reduced fremitus; large effusion shifts mediastinum away; unilateral + cancer history → malignant
Fever or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics suggests complicated parapneumonic fluid/empyema
Bloody fluid: malignancy (prior cancer, mediastinal mass), embolism, trauma; milky → chyle
Foul-smelling pus after aspiration → **anaerobic empyema**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transudate: altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressure; exudate: increased permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage
Heart-failure transudate: pleural protein <3 g/dL, low LDH and cell count; **glucose equals serum**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Chest radiograph → **ultrasound-guided thoracentesis** for new unexplained, unilateral, or atypical effusion
Classic bilateral heart-failure effusions → diuresis first; sample if fever, asymmetry, or treatment failure
★ **Exudate if any Light criterion** positive; compare paired pleural and serum measurements
Pleural pH, glucose, cell differential, Gram stain/culture; cytology if cancer suspected
Diuresis can create pseudoexudate; serum–pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL supports transudate

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat systemic cause; therapeutic thoracentesis for significant symptoms; avoid rapid excessive drainage
★ Pus, positive Gram stain/culture, **pH <7.20** or glucose <60 → empyema/complicated: chest tube, antibiotics
Loculated infected fluid → intrapleural tPA/DNase; persistent sepsis → VATS evaluation
★ Recurrent symptomatic malignancy → **indwelling pleural catheter** or pleurodesis; trapped lung favors catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, loculation, trapped lung, respiratory compromise
Thoracentesis → pneumothorax, bleeding, reexpansion pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Heart-failure control, prompt pneumonia treatment; ultrasound guidance reduces procedural injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atelectasis: mediastinal shift toward volume loss
Consolidation: increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds
Pneumothorax: hyperresonance rather than dullness

pleural-effusion.evidence: Not checked online; established pleural disease teaching.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.scope: Community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration, atypical pneumonia (Legionella, Mycoplasma)
pneumonia.core: Acute lower respiratory infection with a new infiltrate; severity, acquisition setting, and resistance risks determine disposition and empiric antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, COPD, age, immunosuppression
Dysphagia, absent gag/cough (stroke, dementia, Parkinson), impaired consciousness → aspiration
HAP ≥48 hours hospitalized; VAP ≥48 hours after intubation
Prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics → resistant pathogens

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, cough, sputum, focal crackles; older adults: confusion; children: lower-lobe disease may refer abdominal pain
★ Severe: **hypoxemia, hypotension, tachypnea**, multilobar disease; ventilation or pressors → ICU
Legionella: water exposure, diarrhea, hyponatremia; Mycoplasma: school-age/young adult, indolent dry cough, cold agglutinins
Immunocompromised, diffuse bilateral interstitial/alveolar infiltrates, exertional hypoxemia → **Pneumocystis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar inflammation/exudate → shunt and impaired oxygenation
Chemical aspiration pneumonitis: sterile gastric injury; severity tracks **volume and acidity**; rapid improvement possible

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CXR** first; CT if strong suspicion despite nondiagnostic radiograph
**CURB-65** 0–1 or low PSI → outpatient; severe CAP → blood/sputum cultures, Legionella antigen ± PCR
Low procalcitonin alone does not justify withholding initial antibiotics in radiographically confirmed bacterial CAP
Gram-positive lancet diplococci → **S pneumoniae**: commonest CAP; lobar consolidation, high fever, often post-viral URI
Small gram-negative coccobacilli, smoker/COPD → **H influenzae**

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen, fluids for hypoperfusion; drain empyema; narrow antibiotics to cultures
★ Aspiration pneumonia: usual CAP coverage; **add anaerobic coverage only for abscess/empyema**
Anaerobes: **ampicillin-sulbactam**; older exam questions may expect **clindamycin**, even without abscess
Stable nonsevere CAP: ATS 2025 permits 3–4 days; classic ≥5-day rule remains for severe disease
★ Severe noninfluenza CAP → consider **systemic corticosteroids**; nonsevere CAP → avoid routine steroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Parapneumonic effusion, empyema, bacteremia, respiratory failure, sepsis
S aureus: postinfluenza necrotizing pneumonia; child failing amoxicillin, dense consolidation/effusion
Aspiration (alcoholism, intubation) → **lung abscess**: dependent-segment cavity, air-fluid level, foul sputum
Antibiotic exposure → C difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, smoking cessation, swallowing evaluation
Aspiration/VAP prevention: head elevation 30–45°, oral care, early liberation from ventilation

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: thrombotic risk, pleuritic pain, no infectious source
HF: bilateral edema, elevated JVP, cardiac dysfunction

table.title: Empiric adult regimens
rows: Amoxicillin/clavulanate + azithromycin; doxycycline alternative; or levofloxacin
Antipseudomonal: cefepime, ceftazidime, or piperacillin/tazobactam; usually 7 days

pneumothorax.name: Pneumothorax
pneumothorax.scope: Spontaneous pneumothorax (primary, secondary), tension pneumothorax, needle decompression, chest tube thoracostomy
pneumothorax.core: Pleural air causes acute unilateral pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds; circulatory compromise indicates tension physiology requiring immediate decompression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: tall thin young adults, smoking, family history
Secondary: COPD, cystic fibrosis, PJP, interstitial lung disease; trauma/procedures or positive-pressure ventilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral hyperresonance, dyspnea, asymmetric chest expansion; severity depends on underlying reserve
★ **Hypotension + distended neck veins + unilateral absent breath sounds** → tension; tracheal deviation is late
Ventilated: positive pressure converts occult pneumothorax to tension; sudden desaturation, rising airway pressure, collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of negative pleural pressure permits lung collapse
One-way air entry increases intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and causing obstructive shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable tension suspicion → **clinical diagnosis; no imaging delay**
Stable → upright chest radiograph: visceral pleural line with absent peripheral markings
Bedside ultrasound: absent sliding/B-lines supports; lung point highly specific; absent sliding alone nonspecific
CT for uncertain/complex cases; supine radiograph may show deep sulcus rather than apical air

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tension → **immediate needle or finger thoracostomy**, then chest tube; oxygen and resuscitation
Needle commonly fourth/fifth intercostal space anterior/midaxillary, or second midclavicular; insert above rib
★ Minimal symptoms, stable: primary (any size) or small iatrogenic → **observation**, reliable follow-up
Symptomatic/large primary → aspiration or small-bore chest tube; secondary generally admit, drain if symptomatic/significant
Persistent air leak, recurrence, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupation → VATS bleb treatment/pleurodesis

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, tension progression, recurrence; reexpansion pulmonary edema after drainage
Chest tube → bleeding, infection, organ injury; blocked/clamped drain may recreate tension

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Smoking cessation**; avoid flying until radiographic resolution and clearance
Scuba diving contraindicated without specialist assessment/definitive prevention; counsel recurrence warning symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: pleuritic pain with preserved lung sliding, embolic risk
Giant bulla: intraparenchymal thin wall; CT if stable uncertainty before tube
Tamponade: shock with pericardial fluid rather than unilateral absent ventilation
Massive hemothorax: dullness, collapsed neck veins rather than distended

pneumothorax.evidence: Conservative care checked 2026-10-30: [BTS pleural guideline 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784); tension rescue: established emergency teaching.

polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.name: Polyuria and diabetes insipidus
polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.scope: Central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium, hypercalcemia), water deprivation test, desmopressin response
polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.core: Large-volume dilute urine requires separation of water diuresis from solute diuresis; impaired thirst or water access makes diabetes insipidus dangerous.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Central: sellar surgery/trauma/infiltration; nephrogenic: lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia or inherited defects
Primary polydipsia: excessive voluntary intake, psychiatric disease; osmotic diuresis: diabetes mellitus, mannitol

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria >3 L/day in adults, nocturia, polydipsia; distinguish from frequent small-volume voiding
★ **Hypernatremia with urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg** suggests inadequate antidiuretic effect
Low/low-normal sodium favors excess drinking; dehydration, weakness or altered mentation signals severe water deficit

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient vasopressin signaling prevents collecting-duct aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption
Lithium enters collecting-duct cells through ENaC and impairs concentrating ability

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **24-hour urine volume**; serum Na/osmolality, urine osmolality, glucose, calcium, K, creatinine
Hyperglycemia with concentrated solute-rich urine → osmotic diuresis; no need for water deprivation
★ Stable hypotonic polyuria → **supervised water deprivation followed by desmopressin**, or stimulated copeptin testing
Avoid dehydration testing in existing hypernatremia/volume depletion; partial defects may yield overlapping responses
Established central disease → pituitary MRI and anterior-axis evaluation; check lithium level with exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: Shock → isotonic resuscitation first; then oral/IV free water with serial sodium monitoring
★ Central → **desmopressin**; avoid excess water intake and monitor for hyponatremia
Nephrogenic → remove cause, low-solute diet, thiazide; lithium-associated → amiloride
Lithium toxicity → stop drug, isotonic fluids; severe neurologic effects/impaired clearance → hemodialysis consultation
Primary polydipsia → address cause and supervised intake plan; desmopressin risks water intoxication

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypernatremic encephalopathy, seizures, hypovolemic shock; overly rapid chronic sodium correction → cerebral edema
Desmopressin/excess drinking → hyponatremic seizures; chronic lithium → CKD

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Reliable water access, sick-day plan; lithium renal/electrolyte monitoring and avoidance of volume depletion
Mild lithium DI, intact thirst, normal sodium → **keep drinking**; fluid restriction risks hypernatremic dehydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Overactive bladder/UTI: frequency without increased total volume
Postobstructive diuresis: follows relief of retention; monitor fluid/electrolyte losses

polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.evidence: Testing update checked 2026-10-30: [Endotext AVP deficiency/resistance, 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279011/); classic testing patterns: established teaching.

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.name: Population health and quality improvement
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.scope: Program evaluation, outcome and process measures, health equity, PDSA cycles
population-health-and-quality-improvemen.core: Improve care for a defined population through measurable aims, iterative system changes, and attention to unequal access and outcomes.

rows.label: Principle
items: Population denominator includes eligible people missing visits, not only those receiving care
Equity: stratify outcomes by language, race/ethnicity, geography, disability, insurance, deprivation
Greater relative **primary care investment** improves population health, reduces disparities

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Define **measurable aim**, population, baseline, timeframe; engage patients/frontline staff
★ **PDSA**: plan small change → do → study results → act/adapt before scaling
Stratify measures, address interpreter/transport/cost barriers, monitor unintended consequences

rows.label: Don't
items: Do not assume a favorable outcome proves causation without comparison and context
Avoid blaming individuals for failures created by unreliable workflows

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Run/control charts distinguish routine common-cause variation from special-cause signals over time
Program evaluation: reach, fidelity, effectiveness, cost, sustainability versus original goals
Education program → measure knowledge/behavior change; small cohort cannot detect morbidity/mortality

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Process success ≠ patient benefit**; assess both and choose valid denominators
★ **Risk adjustment** improves comparison; also report disparities so adjustment cannot conceal inequity
Before–after improvement may reflect secular trends, case-mix change, regression to mean

population-health-and-quality-improvemen.evidence: Established quality-improvement and program-evaluation principles; no guideline-dependent thresholds.

post-traumatic-stress-disorder.name: Post-traumatic stress disorder
post-traumatic-stress-disorder.scope: PTSD diagnostic criteria (>1 month: intrusion, avoidance, negative mood/cognition, hyperarousal), acute stress disorder (<1 month), trauma-focused psychotherapy (CBT, EMDR), SSRIs, prazosin for nightmares
post-traumatic-stress-disorder.core: Persistent trauma-linked reexperiencing and avoidance with altered mood and heightened arousal cause functional impairment beyond the immediate stress response.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence; direct, witnessed, or qualifying indirect exposure
Prior trauma, psychiatric illness, repeated exposure, poor social support

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Intrusion**: nightmares, flashbacks, distress with reminders; avoidance of internal/external cues
Negative beliefs, guilt, detachment or trauma amnesia; hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, sleep disturbance
Dissociative subtype: depersonalization or derealization; severe distress may coexist with suicidality

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Persistent dysregulated threat response and impaired contextual extinction of traumatic fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical: ≥1 intrusion, ≥1 avoidance, ≥2 negative mood/cognition, ≥2 arousal symptoms
**>1 month**, impairment, and not better explained by substances or another illness
Assess ongoing danger, self-harm risk, substance use, depression and traumatic brain injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **trauma-focused psychotherapy**: prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or EMDR
★ If medication preferred/needed → **sertraline, paroxetine, or venlafaxine**; premature ejaculation → paroxetine (delays ejaculation)
Prazosin for persistent trauma nightmares; monitor orthostatic hypotension, not an overall PTSD treatment
Avoid benzodiazepines; no established benefit and increased dependence risk
Immediate safety planning and psychiatric hospitalization when imminent self-harm or inability to remain safe

rows.label: Complications
items: Depression, substance use disorders, suicide risk, relationship and occupational impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early practical support, **psychoeducation normalizing trauma reactions**; symptomatic acute stress → trauma-focused CBT
